name: Jade
lede: Jade is a green named for a stone, and the stone is really two unrelated minerals; the word came into English from a Spanish phrase for the flank, because the rock was once worn against kidney pain.

sections.title: Two stones under one name
sections.body:
Jade is not one mineral. Jadeite is the intensely colored stone of Burma, found around Myitkyina in the northern mountains, usually green and sometimes lavender [1]. Nephrite is a different material that is mineralogically no relation: duller, found near Khotan in western China and around the Pacific Rim, in Japan, New Zealand, California and Peru [1]. Our gem page credits the French mineralogist Alexis Damour with separating the two chemically in 1863, a date taken from Wikipedia and not checked in the books [2].

Nephrite is the tougher of the two. Finlay notes that it scarcely breaks under a hammer, although it ranks only 6.5 on the Mohs scale, because its fibers are interwoven [3]. Chemists know the same fibrous mineral family as actinolite, a green amphibole whose name comes from the Greek for *ray*, and which is sometimes called nephrite jade [4]. Neither stone is a pigment of its own; the *Pigment Compendium* treats actinolite only as an occasional trace in other materials [4].

One caution for buyers: Finlay adds that nephrite is often faked and dyed [1]. The word on a shop label has never guaranteed the stone.

sections.title: A flank stone
sections.body:
The English word comes from Spanish [1]. Finlay credits Nicolás Monardes, a sixteenth-century doctor in Seville, who used the stone against kidney trouble and called it *piedra de hijada*, the flank stone [1]. Among the books we hold only Finlay gives this origin, so it rests on one source [1].

The dictionary sense is looser than the stone. Paterson defines jade as a green in various shades, mainly yellowish-green, and jade green as a blue-green or a yellowy green [5]. The same book lists Caledon Jade Green, a synthetic dye discovered in 1920 [6]. So by the twentieth century the name could describe a dye as easily as a rock.

sections.title: The stone of China
sections.body:
Finlay reports that nephrite was believed in ancient China to confer immortality and is still treasured there [1]. Jadeite was highly prized in the imperial China of the nineteenth century [1]. A Chinese interest in green stone shows up in unexpected places: an opal dealer in Coober Pedy guessed that Japanese buyers prefer blue and green opals because the color reminds them of jade, though this is his hunch alone [7].

The tradition is changing. Since a diamond marketing campaign reached China in 1993, Finlay says, 51 per cent of urban couples have swapped the traditional green jade for a diamond as the stone of betrothal [3]. In the English-speaking anniversary lists jade marks the 35th year in the modern list, while the older list gave coral or jade for the same year [8]. Alaska and Wyoming both claim jade as their own stone [8].

sections.title: The jade market in Mandalay
sections.body:
Mandalay is sometimes said to have three colors: red, green and white, for ruby, jade and heroin, as well as for its soil, hills and pagodas [9]. Finlay went to the jade market expecting green and found a pale, white place, full of cutting dust [9]. The jade on offer was poor quality, and the only solid green he saw was the baize of the workers' pool tables [9].

The visit shows how far a market stall can sit from a screen swatch, which stands for the best of the stone and not for the average [1][9].

sections.title: Jade in porcelain and ink
sections.body:
One glaze was made to echo jade. Finlay says the first Tang emperor commissioned imperial celadon makers to make bowls prized for resembling white jade [10]. Chinese collectors also prized the fine web of cracks in the glaze, the crackle, because it looks like the fissures in jade [11][12]. Finlay explains that crackle comes from body and glaze shrinking at different rates in the kiln, and a conservator told her it has to be wrong just enough [11]. See [[celadon]] for the glaze itself.

Jade had other luxury uses. Old Chinese ink recipes listed powdered jade beside musk and pearl, and Finlay pictures an emperor eating with jade chopsticks [13][14].

sections.title: Amulets and cures
sections.body: Birren's survey of amulet wearers records what the stone was thought to do: ease childbirth, cure dropsy, quench thirst and calm a racing heart [15]. These are old beliefs, not medicine. The kidney remedy behind the word *jade* belongs to the same family of claims [1][15].

sections.title: The swatch and the stone
sections.body:
The swatch here, #00A86B, is a vivid bluish green, within three units of the ISCC-NBS block called vivid green [16]. It is bluer than Paterson's yellowish-green jade, and far more saturated than most nephrite [5][16]. Our gem page pairs it with a duller nephrite green and a lavender jadeite, because a single color cannot stand for both stones [17].

Its nearest named colors are [[green-crayola]], [[jade-green]] and [[shamrock-green]], all within about three units [16]. The color has two children, [[deep-jade]] and [[jade-green]] [16]. The nearest cut stone in our gem data is [[gem:jade|jade]] itself, and a daylight [[gem:alexandrite|alexandrite]] green is 9.5 units away [16].

In [[film:hero|Hero]] (2002), a memory of an earlier attempt on the king is shown in a vivid green that our film notes list as jade green [18].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Painters have used this exact green rarely. No painting in our archive of 23,781 has a color within CIEDE2000 4 of it covering at least 1 per cent of its canvas, as photographed [19]. That describes our archive, not painting as a whole. It also contrasts weakly with white, at 3.08 to 1, so a white label on this swatch is hard to read [16].

origin.named_after: Spanish piedra de hijada, 'flank stone' (Finlay, via Monardes of Seville)
origin.first_recorded: as a stone, c. 4700 BC (Hongshan culture, per our library); as a color word, later
origin.source: Finlay, Jewels: A Secret History; Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour

disambiguation.gloss: the grey-green glaze made to look like jade, much paler and greyer

questions.q: How are jadeite and nephrite related?
choices: They are unrelated minerals sold under one name
They are the same mineral from two countries
questions.answer: They are unrelated minerals sold under one name

questions.q: Nephrite is easy to shatter with a hammer.
Why did Chinese collectors prize crackle in celadon glaze?
choices: It resembles the fissures in jade
It shows the glaze is poisonous
questions.answer: It resembles the fissures in jade

openers: Jade is two unrelated stones sharing one name, and the word itself means flank stone.
At Mandalay's jade market the only solid green Finlay saw was a pool table.
